declared.title: Can seeking happiness make people unhappy? [corrected] Paradoxical effects of valuing happiness.

population: US women: 59 adults of the Denver community (Study 1), 69 students (Study 2)

findings.text: Women who valued happiness more reported less happiness, but only when their life stress was low, not when it was high

support.sentence: In Study 1, female participants who valued happiness more (vs. less) reported lower happiness when under conditions of low, but not high, life stress.

findings.text: Women led to value happiness (by reading an article praising it) felt less positive than controls while watching a happy film clip, not a sad one

support.sentence: In Study 2, compared to a control group, female participants who were experimentally induced to value happiness reacted less positively to a happy, but not a sad, emotion induction.

findings.text: That drop went through disappointment at one's own feelings

support.sentence: This effect was mediated by participants' disappointment at their own feelings.

limits: women only, small samples: 59, then 69 split into four groups of about 17 (sizes read in the author manuscript, PMC3160511)
Study 1 is cross-sectional, and its link holds only under low life stress
the induction is one faux newspaper article, measured minutes later during a 2-minute film
no direct or multi-lab replication of Study 2 found (2026-11-22)
the Valuing Happiness Scale used here mixes several things: only 1 of its 3 factors goes with lower well-being (Luhmann 2016)
the lab that proposed the valuing-happiness paradox; 4 other sources of this dossier come from the same network (Mauss, Ford)

acknowledged.changes: the title: the author manuscript (PMC3160511) reads « make people happy? », PubMed marks the title [corrected]; the notice itself is unreadable (APA, 403)
